guides-essential-tools.s30: Why is it the most important?
guides-essential-tools.s31: The biological filter hosts beneficial bacteria that convert dangerous ammonia (fish waste) into nitrite, then into nitrate. Without these bacteria, ammonia rises and kills fish within days.
guides-essential-tools.s32: The bacteria live on surfaces inside the filter — not in the water. Therefore the surface area inside the filtration media (biomedia) determines the filter’s strength — not the external size of the filter.

guides-essential-tools.s43: Aquariums up to 60 L: Internal filter or sponge filter with aeration.
guides-essential-tools.s44: 60–150 L: Hang-on-back (HOB) filter or a powerful internal filter.
guides-essential-tools.s45: Over 150 L: Canister filter or sump.

guides-essential-tools.s50: Most common fish (tilapia, guppy, angelfish, betta) come from tropical environments with temperatures ranging from 24 to 28 °C. Fluctuations in temperature — even within this range — weaken the immune system and increase susceptibility to diseases.

guides-essential-tools.s65: Use dechlorinator before or during the addition of new water to the aquarium — not after. Common products: Seachem Prime, Tetra AquaSafe. Prime is stronger as it also handles chloramines.
guides-essential-tools.s67: Ammonia and nitrite — the most dangerous substances in an aquarium — are colorless and odorless. guides-fish-hiding.s54: When you move a fish to a new aquarium, everything about its environment is unknown: the lighting, the sound, the smell of the water, the filter's movement, and the presence of other fish. This is real stress — its body releases stress hormones and its immunity lowers. Therefore, it's normal — and expected — for it to hide for the first 24 to 48 hours. This is instinctive survival behavior, not illness.

guides-fish-hiding.s75: Some fish establish a territory in the aquarium and chase any fish that approaches. The weaker or smaller fish hides to avoid confrontation. Sudden hiding after adding a new fish is a strong indicator of this reason.
guides-fish-hiding.s76: A cramped or decor-lacking aquarium increases aggression — because territorial fish feel they need to defend their entire space.

guides-fish-hiding.s86: Tiger Barb — aggressive in small numbers
guides-fish-hiding.s90: Observe the aquarium for 10 minutes from a distance — without any intervention
guides-fish-hiding.s132: A fish hiding alone isn't necessarily a sign of illness. However, if the hiding is accompanied by other symptoms, we need to pay attention and assess the full picture before taking any action.
guides-fish-hiding.s133: First step: test for ammonia and nitrite. These cause symptoms similar to illness—lethargy, pale color, gasping at the surface—and are often confused.
guides-fish-hiding.s140: Fins held close to the body
guides-fish-hiding.s144: Any abnormal change on the body
guides-fish-hiding.s146: Spiraling, loss of balance, or swimming sideways
guides-fish-hiding.s147: Check the water first—ammonia and nitrite must be zero.
guides-fish-hiding.s148: Photograph the entire aquarium—with clear lighting from the front.
guides-fish-hiding.s149: Photograph the fish if possible—from the side and from above.
guides-fish-hiding.s150: Observe the other fish—have the symptoms spread?
guides-fish-hiding.s151: Do not add medication without a diagnosis—the wrong medication can harm the biological filter.
guides-fish-hiding.s152: Important: Ammonia and nitrite are colorless and odorless—the water may appear clear but is toxic. Do not judge by appearance. Testing with a kit is the only reliable method.
guides-fish-hiding.s154: When you see a fish hiding, the instinct is to “do something now.” Some of these actions can worsen the situation.
guides-fish-hiding.s155: Do not chase the fish with a net without a strong reason
guides-fish-hiding.s156: Catching causes acute stress to the fish—it can be more harmful than the hiding itself. Only chase if there is a clear and present danger.
guides-fish-hiding.s157: Do not change all the water at once
guides-fish-hiding.s158: A 100% water change shocks the fish with sudden changes in temperature and pH. It can also harm beneficial bacteria. Change only 25% at a time.
guides-fish-hiding.s160: Without a clear diagnosis of the cause, the wrong medication kills beneficial bacteria in the filter and exacerbates the problem. Ammonia and nitrite will rise afterward.
guides-fish-hiding.s161: Do not change the filter, decor, and water on the same day
guides-fish-hiding.s162: Too many changes in one day equals shock to the fish and the biological system. Change one thing, observe the result, then move to the next.
guides-fish-hiding.s163: Do not diagnose based on hiding alone
guides-fish-hiding.s164: Hiding is a symptom—not a diagnosis. The cause could be transport stress, aggression, or an environmental issue. You must differentiate the causes first.
guides-fish-hiding.s165: Do not buy new fish before understanding the problem
guides-fish-hiding.s166: Adding new fish during a crisis increases the stress on the aquarium and can introduce additional diseases—especially if you do not quarantine new fish first.

guides-water-myths.s14: The problem isn’t just that the information is wrong — the problem is that people act on it. When you think clear water = healthy, you don’t test. When you think changing all the water is the solution, you destroy beneficial bacteria. The myth gives you false confidence — that is the real danger.
guides-water-myths.s16: Not testing water because you think you can see it
guides-water-myths.s17: Adding products without understanding what you’re doing

guides-water-myths.s26: Understanding is more important than the product
guides-water-myths.s30: Ammonia and nitrite are the most dangerous substances in a fish tank — they are colorless and odorless. Water can appear perfectly clear and still contain ammonia levels that can kill fish within hours. Clarity only indicates the absence of suspended particles, not the absence of chemical toxins.
guides-water-myths.s32: Ammonia (NH3) — toxic from the first rise
guides-water-myths.s33: Nitrite (NO2) — prevents oxygen transport in the blood
guides-water-myths.s38: Water test kit (API Master Test Kit)
guides-water-myths.s41: Daily for the first month of tank setup
guides-water-myths.s42: Immediately if you notice a change in fish behavior
guides-water-myths.s43: Ammonia = 0. Nitrite = 0. Nitrates = less than 20 ppm. These are the correct numbers — not the water color.
guides-water-myths.s44: Changing all the water is the best solution
guides-water-myths.s45: Myth — and dangerous for the tank
guides-water-myths.s46: A 100% water change causes sudden thermal shock, a sudden pH change, and severe stress on the fish. More importantly: beneficial bacteria live on the surfaces of the gravel and filter — not in the water itself. Changing all the water doesn't destroy the biological cycle but shocks the fish with all these sudden changes.
guides-water-myths.s47: Changing all the water also does not eliminate disease or parasites — these remain on the fish's body and on the tank surfaces. The idea that 'cleaning everything' solves the problem is one of the most harmful myths.
guides-water-myths.s49: Change 25% to 30% of the water weekly — this is the recommended rate
guides-water-myths.s50: Use a dechlorinator before adding new water
guides-water-myths.s51: Ensure the temperature of the new water is close to the tank's temperature
guides-water-myths.s52: Do not clean the gravel and filter on the same day as the water change
guides-water-myths.s53: If ammonia levels are very high, change 50% in two parts, several hours apart
guides-water-myths.s55: Do not change 100% of the water
guides-water-myths.s56: Do not clean the filter with tap water
guides-water-myths.s57: Do not change water and clean gravel on the same day
guides-water-myths.s58: The filter alone is enough — the water doesn't need changing
guides-water-myths.s60: The filter converts ammonia to nitrite, and nitrite to nitrate — but it does not remove nitrates. Nitrates accumulate and cause stress to fish and long-term health problems. The only way to remove nitrates from a closed aquarium is through regular water changes or dense live plants.
guides-water-myths.s61: The biological cycle: Ammonia (NH3) ← Nitrosomonas bacteria ← Nitrite (NO2) ← Nitrobacter bacteria ← Nitrate (NO3). The filter manages the cycle — but it doesn't complete it. Water changes are the only 'exit' for nitrates.
guides-water-myths.s62: What relying solely on the filter causes:
guides-water-myths.s63: Gradual nitrate accumulation — with no obvious symptoms at first
guides-water-myths.s64: Fish appear fine for months, then chronic problems begin
guides-water-myths.s105: Small tanks are harder to manage, not easier. Larger tanks have a natural buffer against sudden chemical changes. If ammonia rises slightly in a 200 L tank, the effect is slow. In a 20 L tank, the same amount of excess food will immediately double the ammonia concentration.

guides-decor-stones.s46: Aquarium Decor & Stones — What’s Safe and What Alters Water
guides-decor-stones.s47: The safe stones for an aquarium are inert stones that do not alter water chemistry: basalt, quartz, travertine, and polished river stones. Avoid marble and limestone as they raise pH. Wash all decor in clean water without soap before placing it in the tank. Aquarium wood is safe but may tint water yellow from tannins — this is normal. guides-decor-stones.s1: What stones are safe for aquariums?
guides-decor-stones.s2: Safe stones are inert rocks that do not alter water chemistry: basalt, quartz, dark sandstone, slate, and polished river stones. Avoid calcareous stones like marble and limestone, which raise pH and hardness.
guides-decor-stones.s3: Does a stone change the water's pH?
guides-decor-stones.s4: Yes, calcareous stones (marble, limestone, coral) raise pH and increase water hardness. Granite, basalt, and polished river stones are inert and do not affect pH.
guides-decor-stones.s5: How do I know if a stone is calcareous?
guides-decor-stones.s6: A simple test: place a drop of white vinegar on the stone. If it fizzes or bubbles — the stone is calcareous and unsuitable for neutral freshwater aquariums. No fizzing = likely safe.
guides-decor-stones.s7: Do I need to wash stones before use?
guides-decor-stones.s8: Yes, always. Wash all decor (stones, wood, sand, glass) with clean, warm water without soap. Soap and detergents kill beneficial bacteria and poison the water. Some stones may need soaking for a day or two to remove dust.
guides-decor-stones.s9: Does aquarium wood discolor the water?
guides-decor-stones.s10: Yes, natural aquarium wood (like driftwood) releases tannins that turn the water a light yellow or brown tea color. This is natural and harmless—it even benefits some tropical fish. To remove the color: soak the wood in hot water for a week before placing it in the aquarium.
guides-decor-stones.s11: What's the difference between natural and artificial decor?
guides-decor-stones.s12: Natural decor (stones, wood, sand) provides a realistic look but requires preparation and may affect water chemistry. Artificial decor (resin, plastic, ceramic) is easier to clean and safe for aquariums if made specifically for them, but looks less realistic.
guides-decor-stones.s13: What is the safe distance between decor and the filter outlet?
guides-decor-stones.s14: Leave at least 5-10 cm between decor and the filter outlet to avoid reducing water flow. A partially obstructed filter is less efficient, leading to ammonia buildup in the aquarium.
guides-decor-stones.s15: How do I clean stones and decor?
guides-decor-stones.s16: For routine cleaning: scrub with an old brush under aquarium water (not tap water) to preserve beneficial bacteria. For deep cleaning: use only hot water without soap, then let it dry before returning it to the aquarium.

guides-new-aquarium-setup.s3: Do I need a filter for the aquarium?
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s4: Yes, a filter is essential in every aquarium. It removes ammonia and harmful substances, maintaining water balance. Without a filter, the water quickly becomes polluted, and the fish will die.
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s6: It depends on the type of fish. Tropical fish (like guppies, mollies, angelfish) need a stable temperature between 24-28 °C. Coldwater fish like goldfish do not need a heater.
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s8: Tap water contains chlorine and chloramine, which kill fish and beneficial bacteria. A dechlorinator neutralizes these substances immediately, making the water safe for fish.
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s10: Water test strips measure ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, and pH. These indicators let you know if the tank is safe before or after adding fish. Without testing, you won't know if danger is lurking.
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s11: What is the order for setting up the aquarium?
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s12: 1) Clean the aquarium with water only. 2) Add washed gravel. 3) Install the filter and heater. 4) Fill with water and add dechlorinator. 5) Turn on the filter. 6) Wait 3-7 days for the nitrogen cycle. 7) Test the water. 8) Add fish gradually.
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s14: The most common mistakes include: adding fish immediately without waiting for the nitrogen cycle, not using a dechlorinator, overfeeding, buying too small an aquarium, and not testing the water regularly.
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s15: How many days should I wait before adding fish?
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s16: The minimum is 3 days if you use a bottled beneficial bacteria starter, and 7-14 days without it. It's best to test the water first: when ammonia and nitrite levels are zero, the tank is ready.
guides-new-aquarium-setup.s17: Clean the aquarium and choose its location

guides-water-test-guide.s1: What Do Aquarium Water Test Strips Measure?
guides-water-test-guide.s2: Aquarium water test strips measure: Ammonia (NH3), Nitrite (NO2), Nitrate (NO3), pH, and sometimes Chlorine and Hardness. These are the primary indicators of aquarium water health.
guides-water-test-guide.s3: What Does Ammonia Mean and When Is It Dangerous?
guides-water-test-guide.s4: Ammonia is produced from fish waste and leftover food. Even 0.25 ppm causes stress to fish. Above 1 ppm is a real danger. A safe reading is zero ppm in a mature tank.
guides-water-test-guide.s5: What's the Difference Between Nitrite and Nitrate?
guides-water-test-guide.s6: Nitrite (NO2) is much more dangerous than Nitrate (NO3). Nitrite prevents blood from carrying oxygen and kills fish quickly. Nitrate is less dangerous and is reduced by regular water changes.
guides-water-test-guide.s7: What is the Correct pH for an Aquarium?
guides-water-test-guide.s8: Most freshwater fish require a pH between 6.8-7.5. Tropical fish like guppies and tetras prefer 7.0-7.2. A sudden pH change of more than 0.5 can shock the fish.
guides-water-test-guide.s9: What Should I Do If Ammonia Levels Rise?
guides-water-test-guide.s10: Immediately: Change 25-30% of the water. Stop feeding for a day or two. Check the filter and ensure it's running. Add an emergency ammonia remover temporarily. Test the water again after 24 hours.
guides-water-test-guide.s11: Are Strips Suitable for Beginners, or Do I Need a Meter?
guides-water-test-guide.s12: Strips are very suitable for beginners and sufficient for daily use. Digital meters are more accurate for pH and conductivity, but strips provide adequate results to know if the situation is dangerous or safe.
guides-water-test-guide.s13: How Often Should I Test My Aquarium Water?
guides-water-test-guide.s14: In the first few months: At least weekly. After the tank is established: Every two weeks. When adding new fish or noticing strange behavior: Immediately. Always test one day after a water change.

guides-filter-media.s44: The Most Important Rule: Never replace all media at once

guides-quarantine.s4: Two weeks to protect the entire tank from one disease
guides-quarantine.s5: A quarantine tank is not a luxury — it’s essential for anyone adding new fish. One sick fish without quarantine can spread disease to the entire tank within days.
guides-quarantine.s8: What you need for a simple quarantine tank

guides-quarantine.s12: Place it in the main tank a week before use to activate bacteria

guides-quarantine.s16: The sick or nervous fish jumps. A cover protects and reduces stress
guides-quarantine.s20: Add fish slowly — gradually mix water over 30 minutes. Monitor breathing and movement
guides-quarantine.s23: Check daily: spots, symptoms, appetite. If anything appears — start treatment immediately

guides-quarantine.s40: Accurately identify the type of symptom

guides-feeding-table.s5: Overfeeding spoils the water faster than anything else
guides-feeding-table.s6: The golden rule: what the fish eat in two minutes is the limit. Anything left in the water breaks down, raises ammonia, and destroys the biological cycle.
guides-feeding-table.s9: The right amount based on fish size
guides-feeding-table.s10: There is no fixed gram amount – the rule is two minutes. The fish size determines how many pellets to start with.
guides-feeding-table.s19: Larger pellets suitable for mouth size
guides-feeding-table.s24: Observe over two minutes – what remains = what was eaten

guides-feeding-table.s48: A day without food once a week benefits the aquarium: it gives the filter time to recover and reduces accumulated food residue in the gravel. Healthy fish tolerate it without problems.

guides-water-change-schedule.s5: Not all clear water means it doesn't need changing.
guides-water-change-schedule.s6: Water that appears clean might be full of nitrates and ammonia without you realizing it. The AQUAVO guide provides a clear schedule based on your aquarium size, showing when the water desperately needs refreshing.
guides-water-change-schedule.s7: Who is this for: Every aquarium owner who wants to keep their fish healthy.
guides-water-change-schedule.s9: Why is Regular Water Change Important?
guides-water-change-schedule.s10: The filter removes solid waste, but it doesn't remove nitrates. Nitrates accumulate silently, weakening the fish and encouraging algae growth. Regular water changes are the only natural way to get rid of them.
guides-water-change-schedule.s12: Nitrates build up every week, even if you don't see a visible difference.
guides-water-change-schedule.s14: Old water gradually becomes acidic, affecting the health of fish and corals.
guides-water-change-schedule.s16: Some minerals are consumed by aquatic life and are not added by the filter.
guides-water-change-schedule.s18: Old water increases cortisol levels in fish, weakening their immune system.
guides-water-change-schedule.s19: The Right Schedule for Your Aquarium Size
guides-water-change-schedule.s20: There isn't one schedule that fits all. Aquarium size, fish count, and daily feeding all affect how quickly nitrates accumulate.
guides-water-change-schedule.s28: Small tanks are affected quickly — don't neglect water changes.
guides-water-change-schedule.s34: The ideal size for beginners — relatively stable.
guides-water-change-schedule.s38: Larger aquariums are more forgiving — but don't go longer than two weeks.
guides-water-change-schedule.s39: This is a basic schedule. If you have an overstocked tank or feed heavily, increase the frequency by a day or two.
guides-water-change-schedule.s40: When does the water cry out for a refresh?
guides-water-change-schedule.s41: These signs indicate that nitrates have reached a dangerous level or the water is losing its balance. If you see any of them, change the water now.
guides-water-change-schedule.s43: Accumulation of protein and organic matter — a clear sign the water is unhealthy.
guides-water-change-schedule.s45: Organic acids accumulate and gradually change the water color.
guides-water-change-schedule.s47: Low oxygen or ammonia buildup — change the water immediately and test it.
guides-water-change-schedule.s49: Healthy water has no smell. An odor indicates excessive organic buildup.
guides-water-change-schedule.s51: Algae thrive on nitrates. If they bloom suddenly, the water needs changing.
guides-water-change-schedule.s52: Fish are lethargic or not eating
guides-water-change-schedule.s53: Poor water quality affects appetite and activity — don't delay.
guides-water-change-schedule.s54: Steps for a proper water change
guides-water-change-schedule.s55: An incorrect change can shock the fish more than old water. Follow this order.
guides-water-change-schedule.s58: The new water must be within ±1 degree of the tank's temperature. Temperature differences shock fish.
guides-water-change-schedule.s60: Turn off the heater and filter
guides-water-change-schedule.s61: It's important to turn them off before lowering the water level — an exposed heater can burn out.
guides-water-change-schedule.s64: Use the siphon to go over the gravel and remove waste with the water at the same time.
guides-water-change-schedule.s67: Don't pour quickly. Pour gently on the side or onto a rock to avoid disturbing the gravel.
guides-water-change-schedule.s70: Tap water contains chlorine. Add dechlorinator to the new water just before or immediately after adding it.
guides-water-change-schedule.s72: Turn on the filter and heater
guides-water-change-schedule.s73: Wait 10 minutes after finishing the change before turning them back on.

guides-happy-fish-signs.s3: Healthy fish communicate through their bodies — if you know how to listen.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s4: You don't need a lab to know your fish's condition. Two minutes a day observing their movement and behavior is enough to detect any problem before it becomes a crisis.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s7: 6 Signs Your Fish Are Doing Well
guides-happy-fish-signs.s8: These signs indicate the aquarium is running smoothly and doesn't require intervention:
guides-happy-fish-signs.s11: Healthy fish swim in a straight line without deviation or wobbling. If it moves naturally without effort — good.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s14: Fish come to the surface or swim towards food quickly. Repeated refusal to eat is an early sign of a problem.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s16: Its colors are clear and stable
guides-happy-fish-signs.s17: Pale colors or the appearance of white or dark spots require review. Natural colors = natural health.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s20: Folded fins or fins stuck to the body mean stress or illness. Open fins = comfort and stability.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s22: Explores and does not hide constantly
guides-happy-fish-signs.s23: Healthy fish are curious and move around the aquarium. Constant hiding or gathering in a corner needs attention.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s25: Its breathing is calm and regular
guides-happy-fish-signs.s26: Very rapid gill movement means lack of oxygen or stress. Calm and regular breathing = a good health indicator.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s30: Observe each fish swimming. Note any strange movement or new spots.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s33: Did it not eat or not come to the surface? This is the first indicator of a health problem.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s35: Check the glass and the bottom
guides-happy-fish-signs.s36: Any white spots, new algae, or a fish on the bottom without movement.
guides-happy-fish-signs.s38: Fish at the surface gasping for air
guides-happy-fish-signs.s39: Lack of oxygen — check ventilation and temperature immediately
guides-happy-fish-signs.s41: Sign of external parasites — isolate and examine
guides-happy-fish-signs.s42: Swelling of the body or abdomen
guides-happy-fish-signs.s43: Possible constipation or internal infection — requires diagnosis
guides-happy-fish-signs.s44: Small white spots like salt on the body
guides-happy-fish-signs.s45: Ich — a common parasite that needs quick treatment

guides-white-scale.s3: Chalk on the glass is not dirt — it's minerals from the water itself
guides-white-scale.s4: White deposits on the edges of the aquarium and at the waterline are calcium and magnesium. They appear in every aquarium and do not harm the fish — but they can be easily removed without chemicals.
guides-white-scale.s10: At the waterline, water evaporates but calcium remains and accumulates day after day.
guides-white-scale.s13: Every drop that sprays on the glass and dries leaves a mineral trace. Over time, it becomes a visible layer.
guides-white-scale.s16: Tap water in most areas is hard — the higher the GH, the more deposits will form.
guides-white-scale.s20: Dampen a cloth with natural white vinegar. Leave it on the affected area for 5–10 minutes. Wipe gently.
guides-white-scale.s21: A step you must take before any contact with water:
guides-white-scale.s22: After finishing with the vinegar, wipe the area with a cloth dampened with clean regular water — or rinse the glass from the outside before returning the water or fish. Acidic vinegar changes the pH when it enters the aquarium, even in small amounts.
guides-white-scale.s23: ✓ Safe for fish after thorough rinsing
guides-white-scale.s26: Mix one teaspoon of citric acid with a cup of warm water. Use the same method as vinegar. It has a stronger effect on old, hard deposits.
guides-white-scale.s27: ✓ Do not leave it on the silicone for too long
guides-white-scale.s30: Scrape while gradually refilling. Do not try to remove thick, dry layers with the scraper — use vinegar first.
guides-white-scale.s31: ⚠ Do not use a scraper on acrylic aquariums
guides-white-scale.s33: Wipe the waterline once a week before layers accumulate.
guides-white-scale.s34: If GH is too high, reduce water hardness by mixing tap water with distilled water.
guides-white-scale.s35: Adjust the filter outlet so the spray is inside the aquarium, not on the glass.

guides-algae-control.s3: Algae Aren't Your Enemy — They're a Symptom, Not the Cause
guides-algae-control.s4: Every aquarium has algae. The right question is: Why is it growing excessively? If you know the cause, you can stop it without chemicals and without daily scrubbing.
guides-algae-control.s7: 4 Common Types — Each with a Cause
guides-algae-control.s9: Excess light or high nitrates. Scrape the glass + reduce lighting hours.
guides-algae-control.s11: Low light + silicates in the water. Common in new tanks — disappears on its own.
guides-algae-control.s13: Very high nitrates and phosphates + poor flow. Requires intervention: cleaning and improving water circulation.
guides-algae-control.s15: Floating green bacteria. Caused by direct sunlight or overfeeding. Requires UV or shading.
guides-algae-control.s18: 8–10 hours during the day only. Use a timer for consistency. Do not leave the light on 24/7.
guides-algae-control.s20: Two minutes is enough. Uneaten food becomes nitrates — the main fuel for algae.
guides-algae-control.s22: 20–30% weekly removes nitrates before they accumulate. This is the best preventative treatment.
guides-algae-control.s24: Nerit snails, Otocinclus catfish, Amano shrimp — they eat algae naturally without chemicals.
guides-algae-control.s27: A light film on the glass after a week
guides-algae-control.s28: Scrape it off and continue your routine — not a problem.
guides-algae-control.s31: Reduce lighting by 1 hour, review feeding.
guides-algae-control.s34: Immediate check for nitrates and phosphates + 40% water change.
guides-algae-control.s35: ⚠ Chemical algae killers destroy beneficial bacteria in the filter and harm some fish. Use them only as a last resort, and after rebuilding the biological cycle.
guides-algae-control.s36: Your algae doesn't match any type above?
guides-algae-control.s37: Send a photo of your aquarium — we'll identify the type and give you the correct first step.
